items.label: Figure 1
items.caption:
Figure 1. Comparison between the self-attention mechanism and
the proposed convolutional modulation operation. Instead of gen-
erating attention matrices via a matrix multiplication between the
query and key, we directly produce weights using a k × k depth-
wise convolution to reweigh the value via the Hadamard product
(⊙: Hadamard product; ⊗: matrix multiplication).

items.label: Figure 2
items.caption:
Figure 2. Overall architecture of Conv2Former. Like most previous ConvNets and Swin Transformer, we adopt a pyramid structure with
four stages. In each stage, different numbers of convolutional blocks are used. This ﬁgure shows the setting of the proposed Conv2Former-
T, where {L1, L2, L3, L4} = {3, 3, 12, 3}.

items.label: Table 1
items.caption:
Table 1. Brief conﬁgurations of the proposed Conv2Former. We
implement 5 variants with numbers of parameters 15M, 27M,
50M, 90M, and 199M, respectively.

items.label: Table 2
items.caption:
Table 2. Stage comparison with three popular models. Slightly
adjusting the number of convolutional blocks as shown in the last
row improves the performance.

items.label: Figure 3
items.caption:
Figure 3. Spatial encoding process comparison with self-attention and typical convolutional blocks. Our method uses the convolutional
features from the depthwise convolution as weights to modulate the value representations, as shown in the right linear layer in (d).

items.label: Table 4
items.caption:
Table 4. Top-1 accuracy results on ImageNet [15] with pretraining
on the ImageNet-22k dataset. We can observe consistent improve-
ment compared to ConvNeXt. Our Conv2Former-L also performs
better than EfﬁcientNetV2-XL and CoAtNet-3.

items.label: Table 3
items.caption:
Table 3.
Top-1 accuracy result comparison on ImageNet [15].
Compared to previous popular Transformers and ConvNets, our
Conv2Former achieves a surprisingly good results for network
variants with different model sizes.

items.label: Table 5
items.caption:
Table 5. Comparison with the recent state-of-the-art ConvNets
with different kernel sizes. We can see that without any other train-
ing techniques, like re-parameterization or using sparse weights,
our Conv2Former with kernel size 11×11 achieves the best result.
These experiments indicate that our convolutional modulation op-
eration can more efﬁciently encode the spatial information. More
results with different kernel sizes can be found in Sec. 4.3.

items.label: Figure 4
items.caption:
Figure 4. Ablative experiments. For both Conv2Former-T and Conv2Former-B, we can observe a consistent performance improvement
when increasing the kernel size from 5×5 to 21×21. When replacing the Hadamard product with the element-wise summation operation,
the performance drops for all four variants of our Conv2Former.

items.label: Table 6
items.caption:
Table 6. Performance comparison when different fusion strate-
gies are used in our convolutional modulation block. All results
are based on Conv2Former-T. We can see that using the simple
Hadamard product yields the best result.

items.label: Table 7
items.caption:
Table 7. Comparisons among our isotropic Conv2Former, Con-
vNeXt, and ViT. ‘3 Convs’ means that we use three convolutional
layers for patch embedding at the beginning of the network as done
in [14,43,99]. For both the small-sized and base-sized models, our
Conv2Former achieves better results with comparable parameters
and computations to other methods.

items.label: Table 8
items.caption:
Table 8. COCO [48] object detection and instance segmentation
results using Mask R-CNN [29] and Cascade Mask R-CNN [6].
We report results using the ImageNet-1k dataset pretrained mod-
els.

Table 9. Comparisons with Swin-T and ConvNeXt on the ADE20k
dataset [97]. For all results, we use UperNet [82] as the decoder.
At all model sizes, our Conv2Former achieves the best results.
